description: Track economic, political, social and international change across seven decades of US history.
content_html:
Thinking Thematically: Change and Continuity Across Seven Decades

Studying the USA from 1929 to 2000 means tracking change and continuity across four interconnected areas: the economy, politics, society and foreign policy. Examiners reward students who can synthesise across the period — spotting patterns, turning points, and areas where things stayed the same despite surface changes. This lesson helps you build those connections.

The Economy: From Depression to Superpower

The American economy in 1929 was a capitalist market economy with minimal federal government intervention. The Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression shattered confidence in laissez-faire economics — the belief that markets regulate themselves best without government interference. Roosevelt’s New Deal permanently expanded the federal government’s economic role. The Second World War delivered the full employment the New Deal had not: by 1944 unemployment was below 2 per cent. Post-war prosperity (1945–1970) produced the world’s largest consumer economy.

Key Fact

Economic continuity: the USA remained a capitalist economy throughout 1929–2000. Economic change: the federal government’s role expanded dramatically — from Hoover’s laissez-faire to Roosevelt’s New Deal (1933), Johnson’s Great Society (1965), and Reagan’s rollback of welfare spending (1981). Reagan shifted the dial back towards free markets, but the New Deal’s Social Security Act remained in place.

Politics: From Small Government to Big Government and Back

American politics between 1929 and 2000 was shaped by a fundamental debate about the role of federal government. Hoover represented the old tradition of minimal intervention. Roosevelt broke that tradition decisively with the New Deal. After the Second World War, Truman, Kennedy and Johnson expanded federal responsibility further — civil rights legislation, Medicare, Medicaid, federal education funding. Then Reagan led a conservative revolution from 1981 that sought to reverse this trend, cutting taxes and deregulating industries. Clinton’s “Third Way” in the 1990s accepted the broad framework of both: market economics plus a safety net.

Political scandal was a recurring feature of the period. Harding’s Teapot Dome scandal (1924) predated the period, but Watergate (1972–74) resulted in the first presidential resignation. The Iran-Contra affair (1986–87) — in which Reagan administration officials secretly sold arms to Iran and used the proceeds to fund Nicaraguan rebels — damaged Reagan’s second term. Clinton’s impeachment (1998) showed that personal conduct had become a political weapon. Each scandal reinforced public cynicism about government, but the constitutional system survived each test.

Society: How Much Did America Change?

Social change was profound but uneven. African Americans moved from the legal basis of the Jim Crow system (which dated from the post-Civil War era) to federal civil rights protection by 1968 — a transformation in law. But economic and social equality remained incomplete: unemployment rates among Black Americans remained roughly double white rates throughout the period. Women gained legal equality in employment and reproductive rights, yet faced a glass ceiling in corporate and political leadership. The uneven pace of change is itself an argument you can deploy in extended responses.

Key Fact

Between 1929 and 2000, significant social changes included: civil rights legislation (1964–68); women’s legal equality (Equal Pay Act 1963, Roe v Wade 1973); media transformation (radio to TV to internet); and the rise of a mass consumer middle class. Persistent inequalities included: racial economic gaps; gender pay gap; poverty (Harrington counted 40–50 million poor in 1962); and the gap between suburban prosperity and urban poverty.

Foreign Policy: From Isolation to Superpower

In 1929 the USA was not formally isolationist but it avoided European entanglements. Pearl Harbor (December 1941) ended that era permanently. After 1945, the USA was irreversibly a global superpower: founding member of the UN and NATO, the world’s largest economy, possessor of nuclear weapons. The Cold War structured US foreign policy from 1947 until 1991 — every military intervention (Korea, Vietnam, Gulf War) was framed through the lens of containing communism or managing the post-Cold War order. The end of the Cold War in 1991 left the USA as the world’s sole superpower, but the Gulf War demonstrated that the threats requiring military response had changed.

Major turning points include: 1933 (New Deal — federal government permanently expanded); 1941 (Pearl Harbor — isolationism ended); 1954 (Brown v Board — legal segregation challenged); 1963-68 (civil rights legislation — Jim Crow ended legally); 1974 (Nixon resignation — constitutional checks on presidential power tested); 1980-81 (Reagan revolution — ideological shift to conservatism); 1991 (Gulf War + USSR dissolved — Cold War ended). When writing extended essays, use these as pegs to organise your argument about how much change occurred and what caused it.
exam_tip_html: For 16-mark period essays, the examiners will reward you for showing change across the whole period, not just focusing on one decade. Use the four themes (economy, politics, society, foreign policy) as a mental checklist. For each, identify: (1) what it looked like in 1929; (2) the key turning point(s); (3) what it looked like by 2000; (4) what stayed the same (continuity). Your conclusion must make a substantiated overall judgement about how much change occurred and which factor drove it most significantly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The American economy shifted from minimal-government capitalism (1929) through the New Deal expansion of federal power (1933) to post-war prosperity and Reagan’s conservative rollback (1981) — a pendulum of change and partial continuity. Pearl Harbor (1941) ended US isolationism permanently, making the USA a global superpower after 1945.
  • Political change was marked by a debate about federal government’s role. Key turning points: New Deal (1933), Great Society (1965), Reagan revolution (1981). Political scandals (Watergate 1974, Clinton impeachment 1998) tested but did not break the constitutional order.
  • Social change was profound but uneven: civil rights legislation ended Jim Crow legally by 1968, women gained legal equality in employment and reproductive rights, but racial economic inequality and poverty persisted. By 2000, the USA was a transformed but still unequal society.

practice_questions.text: Describe one area of continuity in American politics between 1929 and 2000.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: Names area of continuity (the USA remained a two-party democratic republic; the constitutional checks and balances system; the role of the Supreme Court in striking down unconstitutional legislation; or capitalism as the economic system) AND develops it. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two turning points in the development of the USA between 1929 and 2000.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per turning point. Mastering: e.g. (1) 1941 Pearl Harbor attack ended isolationism and made the USA a permanent global power; (2) The New Deal (1933) permanently expanded the federal government's role in the economy. Developing: Identifies without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the role of the federal government in the US economy changed between 1929 and 1941.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies cause (Wall Street Crash and scale of the Depression made Hoover's laissez-faire approach untenable; mass unemployment, Hoovervilles and bank failures demonstrated market failure; Roosevelt's electoral mandate for action) AND develops the chain of reasoning. Secure: Cause with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Second World War for the USA's role in world affairs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies consequence (USA emerged as global superpower; isolationism ended permanently; founding member of UN and NATO; economic dominance with Marshall Plan; possession of nuclear weapons; permanent military presence abroad) AND develops the chain of effects. Secure: Consequence with development. Developing: Simple point. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of 1941-1945 as a period of change for the development of the USA.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies changes (economic: wartime production ended Depression, full employment; social: women in workforce, Black Americans' wartime contribution and changed expectations; foreign policy: from isolationism to global power, UN, NATO) AND explains significance of the changes both at the time and for the longer-term development of the USA. Secure: Changes identified with explanation. Developing: Describes the period without analysing change. Emerging: Narrative.

practice_questions.text: 'Economic change was more significant than social change in the development of the USA between 1929 and 2000.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues economic change (Depression, New Deal, wartime boom, post-war prosperity, Reaganomics, 1990s tech boom) against social change (civil rights legislation ending Jim Crow; women's rights; counterculture; Stonewall and gay rights; media transformation) and reaches a substantiated judgement about relative significance. Should acknowledge interaction: economic change shaped social possibilities. Secure: Clear argument on both sides. Developing: Describes changes without weighing relative significance. Emerging: Narrative.

knowledge_checks.q: Which event ended the USA's isolationist foreign policy permanently?
In which year did the Reagan Revolution shift American politics towards conservatism?
The _____ permanently expanded the federal government's economic role after the failures of laissez-faire capitalism in the Depression.
The concept of _____ means identifying where things changed and where they stayed the same across a long period of history.
Match each turning point to the theme it most clearly represents:
right: Social change — legal challenge to segregation
Economic/political change — expanded federal government role

flashcard_questions.q: What is synthesis in historical study?
flashcard_questions.a: Connecting themes across a long period to identify patterns, turning points and areas of continuity.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the long-term impact of the New Deal on American politics?
flashcard_questions.a: It permanently expanded the federal government's economic role, creating the modern welfare state.
The Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one area of continuity in the US economy 1929-2000.
flashcard_questions.a: The USA remained a capitalist market economy throughout the period.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a turning point in history?
flashcard_questions.a: An event or development that marks a decisive shift in direction, after which things are fundamentally different.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one area where racial inequality persisted despite civil rights legislation.
flashcard_questions.a: Black American unemployment rates remained roughly double white rates throughout the period.

flashcard_questions.q: What was Reagan's ideological shift from Johnson's Great Society approach?
flashcard_questions.a: Reagan cut taxes and reduced federal social spending, believing government intervention harmed economic growth.

flashcard_questions.q: What four themes can be used to analyse change in the USA 1929-2000?
flashcard_questions.a: Historians analyse the economy, political institutions, social equality and foreign policy to track change and continuity across the period.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of how the Cold War structured US foreign policy between 1947 and 1991.
flashcard_questions.a: Every military intervention (Korea, Vietnam, Gulf War) was framed through the lens of containing communism.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to identify change and continuity and explain which factors caused them, rather than listing events in chronological order.
The boundary between what the federal government actively does for citizens and what is left to individuals, states and the market.
The idea that society moves forward in one direction (e.g. towards greater equality) but at different speeds for different groups and with temporary reversals.
A foreign policy of avoiding alliances and involvement in the affairs of other countries, which characterised US policy before 1941.
